keyConcepts.title: Goals of secure communication
keyConcepts.text: **Confidentiality** (only the intended parties can read it), **message integrity** (not altered), **end-point authentication** (confirming who's on the other end) and **operational security** (firewalls, IDS).

keyConcepts.title: Symmetric key cryptography
keyConcepts.text: The same secret key encrypts and decrypts. It evolved from Caesar and substitution ciphers to block ciphers like **AES**. **CBC** XORs each block with the previous ciphertext so identical blocks encrypt differently.

keyConcepts.title: Public key cryptography and RSA
keyConcepts.text: Encrypt with the receiver's public key and decrypt with their private key. RSA: n = pq, z = (p−1)(q−1), ed mod z = 1; **c = m^e mod n**, **m = c^d mod n**. It's secure because factoring n is hard.

keyConcepts.title: Session keys
keyConcepts.text: Public key crypto is slow, so it's used only to send a random symmetric **session key**. Bulk data is then encrypted with fast symmetric crypto (like AES).

keyConcepts.title: Hashes, MACs and signatures
keyConcepts.text: A cryptographic hash makes collisions infeasible. A **MAC** = H(m + shared secret). A **digital signature** = the hash signed with the private key and verified with the public key.

keyConcepts.title: Certificates and CAs
keyConcepts.text: A Certification Authority verifies an identity and signs a certificate binding that identity to its public key (X.509). Browsers trust the CAs' public keys.

keyConcepts.title: End-point authentication
keyConcepts.text: Simple approaches fail to spoofing, eavesdropping and **replay** attacks. A **nonce** (a value used only once) proves the other side is live.

keyConcepts.title: Secure email (PGP)
keyConcepts.text: Sign the message hash with the sender's private key for integrity and authentication; encrypt with a session key, which is encrypted with the receiver's public key, for confidentiality. PGP uses a web of trust.

keyConcepts.title: TLS
keyConcepts.text: Handshake (certificate, pre-master secret, nonces) → master secret → **four keys** → data sent as records with an HMAC and an implicit sequence number. Handshake HMACs and close records stop tampering and truncation.

keyConcepts.title: IPsec and VPNs
keyConcepts.text: **ESP** provides confidentiality, integrity and authentication. **Tunnel mode** wraps the whole original datagram (protocol 50). Security associations are one-way and set up by **IKE**.

keyConcepts.title: Wireless security
keyConcepts.text: WiFi (WPA2/3): mutual authentication with nonces, then a derived session key, with EAP and RADIUS behind the AP. 4G/5G **AKA** uses the SIM's secret key; 5G encrypts the IMSI.

keyConcepts.title: Firewalls and IDS
keyConcepts.text: Packet filters (per-packet ACLs), stateful filters (connection table) and application gateways. An IDS uses deep packet inspection and is **signature-based** or **anomaly-based**.

flashcards.back: Only the sender and intended receiver can understand the message, which requires encryption.
The message wasn't altered in transit, by accident or on purpose.
Confirming the other party is who they claim to be.
Plaintext: the original message. Ciphertext: the encrypted, unreadable version.
Symmetric: both sides share one secret key. Public key: a public key anyone can use plus a private key only the owner knows.

flashcards.front: Why is a monoalphabetic cipher easy to break?
flashcards.back: Statistical analysis: letter frequencies (e, t) and common letter groups (the, ing) reveal the mapping.
Known-plaintext: the attacker knows some plaintext/ciphertext pairs. Chosen-plaintext: the attacker can pick plaintext and see its ciphertext.
Encrypts fixed-size blocks (like 128 bits) with a key-driven one-to-one mapping, e.g. AES.
128, 192 or 256 bits (with 128-bit blocks). DES's 56-bit key is no longer secure.
**c(i) = K_S( m(i) XOR c(i−1) )**, starting from a random IV sent in the clear. Identical plaintext blocks encrypt differently.
Pick primes p, q; n = pq; z = (p−1)(q−1); choose e coprime to z; find d with ed mod z = 1. Public key (n, e), private key (n, d).
Encrypt: **c = m^e mod n**. Decrypt: **m = c^d mod n**.
There's no known fast way to factor a large n into p and q.
A random symmetric key sent encrypted with the receiver's public key, then used to encrypt the actual data quickly.
It's computationally infeasible to find two different messages x and y with H(x) = H(y).

flashcards.front: Why is the Internet checksum a bad cryptographic hash?
flashcards.back: It's easy to find another message with the same checksum (e.g. IOU100.99BOB and IOU900.19BOB).
**H(m + s)**: the hash of the message plus a shared secret s. The receiver recomputes it to check integrity and origin. HMAC is the standard.
The sender encrypts H(m) with their private key; anyone verifies it with the sender's public key. It's verifiable and can't be forged.
A MAC uses a shared secret and no encryption. A signature uses public key crypto and needs a PKI with certificates.
Verifies an entity's identity and issues a signed certificate binding that identity to its public key.
Recording a valid authentication message (even an encrypted one) and replaying it later to impersonate someone.
A number used only once in a lifetime, sent as a challenge to prove the other party is live.
Users vouch for (sign) each other's public keys instead of relying on a central CA.
E_B and M_B (encryption and HMAC keys for client → server), E_A and M_A (for server → client), all derived from the master secret.

flashcards.front: Why does TLS include sequence numbers in the HMAC?
flashcards.back: So an attacker can't reorder, replay or drop records without the HMAC check failing.

flashcards.front: Why are nonces used in the TLS handshake?
flashcards.back: So each session gets different keys, which defeats a connection replay attack.
An attacker ends the session early with a TCP FIN. Defense: a closing TLS record type, so an early FIN is noticed.
AH: authentication and integrity only. ESP: authentication, integrity AND confidentiality (much more widely used).
The whole original datagram is encrypted inside a new IP datagram between the two gateways, with protocol number 50 (ESP).
A one-way IPsec logical connection, identified by an SPI and stored in the SAD with its algorithms and keys.
SPD (Security Policy Database): which datagrams get IPsec and which SA to use. SAD: how, meaning the keys and algorithms for each SA.
Internet Key Exchange. It automatically creates SAs: phase 1 builds a secure IKE SA (Diffie-Hellman), phase 2 creates IPsec SAs in each direction.
Badly flawed encryption that could be broken in minutes. It was replaced by WPA, WPA2 and WPA3.
Discovery, mutual authentication and key derivation, session key distribution to the AP, then encrypted communication (AES).

flashcards.front: 4G AKA: how does the network authenticate the device?
flashcards.back: The HSS computes an expected response with the shared SIM key; the MME compares it with the device's response.
The IMSI is encrypted with the home network's public key, defeating IMSI catchers (fake base stations).
Traditional: judges each packet alone using ACL rules. Stateful: tracks TCP connections and only allows packets that belong to a real connection.
An app-specific server that all of an app's traffic must pass through, allowing per-user policy. You need one gateway per application.
A lower-security zone holding public servers (web, DNS), protected by the packet filter and monitored by an IDS.
Signature: matches known attack patterns but can't catch new attacks. Anomaly: flags unusual traffic and can catch new attacks, but distinguishing normal from abnormal is hard.

quiz.q: Which security property ensures a message wasn't changed in transit?
quiz.explain: Integrity is about detecting alteration. Confidentiality is about keeping the content secret.

quiz.q: How does Alice send a confidential message to Bob using public key cryptography?
options: Encrypt it with Bob's public key
Encrypt it with Alice's private key
Encrypt it with Bob's private key
Encrypt it with Alice's public key
quiz.explain: Only Bob's private key can decrypt something encrypted with his public key.

quiz.q: RSA with p = 5, q = 7 and e = 5. Which d works?
Why are session keys used with RSA?
options: RSA is slow, so it only encrypts a symmetric key used for the bulk data
Symmetric encryption is less secure, so it's avoided
quiz.explain: Symmetric ciphers like AES are much faster; RSA safely delivers their key.

quiz.q: What problem does cipher-block chaining solve?
options: Identical plaintext blocks producing identical ciphertext blocks
quiz.explain: XOR-ing each block with the previous ciphertext block (starting with a random IV) hides repeated patterns.

quiz.q: How is a message authentication code (MAC) computed?
options: Hash of the message combined with a shared secret: H(m + s)
Encrypting the message with a private key
The Internet checksum of the message
Encrypting the message with a public key
quiz.explain: Only someone who knows the shared secret s can produce a matching MAC.

quiz.q: How does Bob create a digital signature for message m?
options: Encrypt H(m) with his private key
Encrypt H(m) with his public key
Encrypt m with Alice's public key
quiz.explain: Anyone can verify it with Bob's public key, but only Bob's private key could have created it.

quiz.q: What problem do certificates and CAs solve?
options: Verifying that a public key really belongs to who it claims to
quiz.explain: Without certification, Trudy could hand out her own public key while claiming to be Bob (the pizza prank).

quiz.q: Which authentication protocol defeats playback attacks?
quiz.explain: A fresh nonce proves Alice is live; a recorded response won't match a new nonce.

quiz.q: In TLS, why do the client and server exchange HMACs of all handshake messages at the end?
options: To detect tampering, such as an attacker removing strong algorithms from the list
quiz.explain: The algorithm list is sent in the clear, so this final check catches any man-in-the-middle changes.

quiz.q: What stops an attacker from reordering TLS records?
options: Sequence numbers included in each record's HMAC
quiz.explain: Each side tracks the expected sequence number, so a reordered or replayed record fails the HMAC check.
AH provides only authentication and integrity; ESP adds encryption and is far more widely used.

quiz.q: In IPsec tunnel mode, what's in the new outer IP header?
options: The addresses of the two tunnel endpoints (gateways) and protocol 50
The original source and destination hosts
quiz.explain: The original datagram, including its addresses, is encrypted inside the payload.

quiz.q: What advantage does a stateful packet filter have over a traditional one?
options: It only allows packets that belong to tracked TCP connections
quiz.explain: A traditional filter could let in a crafted packet with ACK = 1. A stateful filter checks its connection table first.

quiz.q: What is a key weakness of signature-based intrusion detection?
options: It can't detect new attacks that have no signature yet
quiz.explain: Anomaly-based IDS can catch new attacks, but it's hard to separate unusual-but-normal traffic from real attacks.

quiz.q: What does 5G do to protect a user's IMSI?
options: Encrypts it with the home network's public key
quiz.explain: In 4G the IMSI was sent in the clear, which made fake base stations (IMSI catchers) possible.
